paras: The Durham Brothers turpentine still whitecapping case was the arrest in late August 1910 of two white men, William McLemore and Frank Parker, accused of driving a Black worker away at gunpoint from a turpentine still about eight miles south of Poplarville, Mississippi. The Hattiesburg News, the only paper found to report the case, presented the arrests as a hoped-for end to months of terror among the still's Black workers and to a labor shortage costly to the turpentine business.

According to a Poplarville dispatch dated August 31, there had been "constant terror" for several months among the Black workers at the Durham Brothers' still, which the dispatch attributed to "white cappers." The trouble came during the turpentine harvest, when the dispatch said a scarcity of labor could cost "thousands of dollars in a very short time."

V. D. Durham, a member of the firm, said he had "positive proof" that McLemore and Parker had marched one of his Black hands away from his place at night at the point of shotguns. By Durham's account, the men would not let the worker collect his clothing or see Durham before he was taken off. The worker was not named, and the coverage does not say what became of him or give the date of the incident.

On a charge of white-capping sworn to by Durham, Sheriff Rouse arrested McLemore and Parker on the night before the dispatch, about August 30. A preliminary trial was set for the end of that week, but no report of the hearing or of any later outcome was found.

The Hattiesburg News ran the story on page four under the headline "Charged With White Capping the Negroes." The dispatch told the story from the employer's side, resting the account of the removal on Durham's sworn charge and expressing the hope that the arrests would "end this trouble" because of the cost of lost labor. The worker's own account does not appear, and no Black-press coverage of the case or a second white paper carrying it was found.

accounts.label: Employer's sworn charge (Poplarville dispatch)
accounts.gist: V. D. Durham said he had positive proof that McLemore and Parker marched one of his Black hands away at night at shotgun point; the dispatch tied the arrests to months of terror among Black workers at the still.

framing.detail: The headline 'Charged With White Capping the Negroes' and the hope that the arrests would 'end this trouble' treated the case chiefly as a threat to turpentine labor and its owners' profits.

record_check.dossier: whitecapping: the men were charged with white-capping, and the dispatch attributed months of terror at the still to 'white cappers'
Arrests about 1910-08-30 ('last night' before the Aug. 31 dispatch); terror over 'several months'; the forced march itself is undated
William McLemore and Frank Parker, two white men (accused)
Two men acting at night (a whitecapping band of two), not a mob

record_check.record: Two white men ... Sheriff arrested them on whitecapping charges.
record_check.dossier: Accurate, but should note that the act rests on Durham's sworn charge, the still lay about 8 miles south of Poplarville, and a preliminary trial was set (no outcome found)

info: Terror at the still had gone on 'for several months'; the arrests were made 'last night' before the Aug. 31 dispatch, i.e. about Aug. 30, 1910; the date of the forced march is not given beyond 'in the night time'.
Durham Brothers' turpentine still, about 8 miles south of Poplarville
One unnamed Black worker ('one of his negro hands') of V. D. Durham; more broadly 'the negroes' at the still
Two white men, William McLemore (printed 'MrLemore' in the page OCR) and Frank Parker, charged with whitecapping; the dispatch attributes the months of terror to 'white cappers'
